citations.excerpt: What happens in SE? Code is written! Programming is crucial to SE. But SE is more than programming.
Draw an Activity-on-node graph for this project... [6 marks] ... Find the estimated duration of the project. [5 marks]

recall.a: Misread dependencies; forgetting durations on the graph; arithmetic slips in passes; claiming duration = sum of all tasks; no verification of path sum.
recall.q: List four ways students lose planning marks.

sections.heading: How planning marks are lost
bullets: Misreading the dependency table (especially multi-predecessor tasks like E after B,C).
Drawing the graph without durations, then having nowhere to put ES/EF/LS/LF.
Backward-pass errors: taking max instead of min over successors.
Stating project duration as the sum of all task durations.
Naming a 'critical path' whose activities do not sum to the stated duration.
Iterative-waterfall answers that describe phases but never mention feedback loops or cost of late change.

callout.text: Verification ritual (30 seconds): sum your critical path. If it does not equal your max EF, find the error before writing the final answer. Examiners in 2018-2022 rewarded shown working even when the final path was wrong.

summary: The six classic planning mark-losers — and the 30-second verification ritual that catches most of them.
title: Planning: common exam mistakes

activities.prompt: Project duration equals the sum of all task durations.

distractor.0: Only the critical path's tasks sum to the duration — off-path work overlaps in time. 2022 Project A totals far more than 25 weeks of tasks.

activities.explanation: False. Duration is the longest path through the network, not the sum of everything.
